title: Do You Need a Facade Consultant? Scope, Fees and When Peer Review Pays for Itself

description: Should you hire a facade consultant? See what they do, how they charge and when independent peer review saves more than it costs.

contentSections: The facade is one of the most expensive parts of a building, and one of the most common sources of leaks, delays and disputes. Yet many projects in India reach site with no independent expert checking the facade design.
A facade consultant is that expert. This guide explains what they do, how they charge, when you need one and when you can skip one.
What Is a Facade Consultant?

A facade consultant, also called a facade engineer or building envelope consultant, is an independent specialist who advises on the design, performance and construction of a building's outer skin. They are paid by the client or the architect, not by the company that sells or installs the facade. That independence is the whole point.
What a Facade Consultant Actually Does
Scope varies, but typical services include:

• Concept and design support. Advising on systems, materials and cost early, before design is fixed.
  • Performance specification. Setting targets for wind load, water tightness, thermal performance, acoustics and fire.
  • Tender documents. Writing clear specifications so vendors quote on the same basis.
  • Bid review. Comparing quotes fairly and flagging gaps, such as missing items or weak specifications.
  • Shop drawing review. Checking the contractor's detailed drawings against the design intent.
  • Mock-up and testing oversight. Witnessing tests and approving the full size mock-up.
  • Site inspection. Visiting during installation to catch problems early.
  • Handover support. Checking final quality, documentation and warranties.
What Is Facade Peer Review?

Peer review is a lighter service. Instead of managing the whole facade, the consultant reviews a design that someone else created, such as the architect's drawings or the contractor's engineering. They look for risks, gaps and errors, then report back.
Think of it as a second opinion on a major medical decision. It costs far less than full consultancy and can catch expensive mistakes before they are built.
When You Probably Need a Consultant

• Tall buildings. Wind load, fire rules and movement are more critical as height increases.
  • Complex geometry. Curved, twisted, parametric or custom facades carry higher design and fabrication risk.
  • Large facade area. On big projects, even a small saving or error is multiplied across thousands of square metres.
  • Hospitals, airports, data centres and other critical buildings. Failure costs are high.
  • Unfamiliar systems. If your team has not specified this type of facade before.
  • Tight timelines. Early expert input prevents redesign later.
  • Previous bad experience. If you have faced leaks or delays on past projects.
When You Can Probably Skip One

• Single homes and small villas with standard cladding systems.
  • Repeat designs where the same facade has already been built and tested.
  • Small commercial fit-outs with a trusted specialist and a clear scope.
Even then, a one-time peer review of drawings may be worth it if the facade is a large part of your budget.
How Facade Consultants Charge
Fee structures vary. The most common ones are:

ModelHow it worksBest for
Percentage of facade costFee is a share of the facade package valueFull service on large projects
Fixed feeAgreed amount for a defined scopeClear, bounded scopes
Time basedHourly or daily ratesAdvisory work and peer reviews
Per stageSeparate fees for design, tender, constructionPhased projects
Exact fees depend on project size, complexity and scope. Ask for a proposal that lists deliverables, number of site visits, review rounds and exclusions, so you can compare consultants fairly.
When Does Peer Review Pay for Itself?
Peer review pays off when the cost of one avoided mistake is greater than the fee. Consider what a single error can cost:

• Water leaks that damage interiors and need repeated repair
  • Panels that do not fit and must be remade
  • Fire compliance failures that force material replacement
  • Delays that hold up handover, rent or sales
  • Disputes between the client, contractor and architect

On a large facade, preventing even one of these usually costs far less than the review itself. A simple test: if the facade is a major share of your budget and you cannot personally judge its engineering, an independent review is cheap insurance.
How to Choose a Facade Consultant

• Ask for similar projects they have worked on, in India and in comparable climates.
  • Check that they are independent and take no commission from suppliers.
  • Speak to past clients about responsiveness and site presence.
  • Review a sample report to see how clear and practical it is.
  • Confirm who will actually do the work, not only who presents the pitch.
  • Make sure they understand local codes, including fire and structural requirements.
How a Consultant and a Facade Manufacturer Work Together

A good consultant and a good manufacturer are partners, not rivals. The consultant sets the target and checks quality. The manufacturer engineers, fabricates and installs to meet it. When both are involved early, design changes happen on paper, not on site.
